## February 20, 1952

You were born fourteen days into a new reign. On February 6, 1952, King George VI died in his sleep at Sandringham — a quiet death after a long illness — and a twenty-five-year-old Princess Elizabeth, at that moment on a royal tour in Kenya, learned that she was Queen. The Elizabethan age began while your mother was still weeks away from her due date. Elizabeth II would reign until September 2022 — seventy years — and you would outlast her. You were born into the first fortnight of one of the longest reigns in British history and lived past its end.

**The world you entered was militarized, frightened, and on edge.** The Korean War had been grinding for nineteen months. By February 1952, armistice talks at Panmunjom were stalled — primarily over whether North Korean and Chinese prisoners should be forcibly repatriated, many of whom refused to return. The war that Harry Truman had committed American troops to in a matter of days in June 1950 would not end until July 1953, when you were sixteen months old. More than 36,000 Americans died in it. The war was unpopular, inconclusive, and — unlike the war that ended seven years before your birth — it produced no parade.

**The domestic atmosphere was one of enforced suspicion.** Senator Joseph McCarthy had launched his anti-Communist crusade in February 1950, and by the time of your birth it had metastasized into something that touched nearly every institution in American life: loyalty oaths for civil servants, blacklists in Hollywood, investigations of university professors, neighbors reported by neighbors. The Red Scare was not a political abstraction in 1952; it was the air people breathed. The Army-McCarthy hearings that finally broke McCarthy's credibility were still two years away. You spent your earliest years in a country that was, in a specific and measurable sense, afraid of itself.

**Eight months after you were born**, on November 1, 1952, the United States detonated Ivy Mike at Enewetak Atoll in the Pacific — the first true hydrogen bomb. Its yield was 10.4 megatons, roughly 450 times the force of the bomb that destroyed Hiroshima. The island it vaporized had been 1,700 yards across. The Soviet Union tested its own hydrogen bomb in August 1953. In the year of your birth, the theoretical capacity for human self-destruction crossed a threshold it had not previously reached, and the Cold War that shaped your entire childhood, adolescence, and early adulthood was conducted in the shadow of that threshold from that point forward.

**One other shadow fell over early childhood in ways now mostly forgotten:** polio. In 1952, the United States suffered its worst polio epidemic on record — nearly 58,000 cases reported, more than 3,000 deaths, thousands more left with permanent paralysis. For a parent of a young child in 1952, polio was not a distant medical statistic; it was the reason children were kept away from public swimming pools in summer, the reason playgrounds emptied during outbreaks. The Salk vaccine would not be announced until April 1955, when you were three. The relief that announcement produced in American parents was something the people who lived through it never forgot.

---

**What seventy-four years look like from here:**

You were ten during the Cuban Missile Crisis — old enough to understand, from adult faces and hushed conversations, that something genuinely terrifying was happening, without fully grasping that the world was as close to nuclear exchange as it would ever come. You were eleven when Kennedy was shot. Sixteen when 1968 arrived with the murders of Martin Luther King Jr. and Robert Kennedy, the Chicago convention, cities in flames.

You were seventeen when humans walked on the Moon — and that moment, unlike the crises, was unambiguously good. A genuinely shared collective astonishment that a species that had invented the airplane sixty-six years earlier had now left the planet.

You were twenty-two during Watergate, which taught your generation something specific about the relationship between institutions and the truth. You were twenty-seven during the Iranian Revolution and the oil shock, thirty-seven when the Berlin Wall fell, forty-nine on September 11. You have been through the entire arc of the nuclear age — from its most dangerous early years through the Cold War through the post-Cold War assumption that the worst was behind us, to a present in which that assumption has been substantially revised.

---

You entered a world of typewriters, party-line telephones, and a polio epidemic. You have now lived into the age of artificial intelligence, genomic medicine, and a global internet. The distance between those two points is not merely technological; it is civilizational. And you made the crossing having started fourteen days into the reign of a queen who would come to represent continuity itself — and then watching her go first.
